Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Setting: Greek myth as told in Homer, Hesiod and the Greek tragedies, depicted faithfully to those stories: bronze armour, crested helmets, round aspis shields, linen chitons, black ships, the wine-dark Aegean sea, white limestone, temples, cypress, smoke and fire.

Subject: A training dummy in a sandy Greek practice yard by the sea: a figure of straw and sacking lashed to a wooden post, wearing a dented old bronze helmet and a battered round shield, spear-holes in its chest.

Composition: a head-and-shoulders portrait, from a low angle looking up. Light and colour: icy dawn blue. Presence: an ordinary, humble presence at a modest scale. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: a head-and-shoulders portrait
composition.angle: from a low angle looking up
composition.power: an ordinary, humble presence at a modest scale

common.name: Common frame
common.prompt:
A blank, empty trading-card frame template for a card game based on the Odyssey and Greek myth, seen perfectly flat and straight-on, filling the whole image edge to edge, portrait orientation. Layout from top to bottom: a narrow horizontal title bar across the top with a round empty medallion at its right end; below it a large rectangular art window taking up about the upper half of the card, filled with solid flat pure black (#000000) with crisp straight edges; below that a thin horizontal type bar; below that a large empty rectangular text box of pale aged parchment; at the bottom right a small empty plaque overlapping the corner of the text box. The title bar, medallion, type bar, text box and plaque are completely blank. Style: a rustic, retro 1990s hand-painted trading-card frame, gouache and ink texture, worn and weathered like an old printed card, muted colours, matte with no glossy highlights, no glow, no light rays, no sky, symmetrical with clean edges. Absolutely no text, no letters, no numbers, no symbols, no logo, no watermark, and nothing inside the black window.

Common rarity: a plain frame of dark weathered bronze and grey stone with a simple thin Greek key (meander) border, modest and unornamented.
Heavily played condition: whitened, rounded and slightly dog-eared corners, frayed edges, a soft crease or two across the frame, small scuffs and scratches, light grime and faded ink, like a much-loved card shuffled hundreds of times. The wear is on the frame only; the black art window stays solid, untouched black.

fig_lotus.name: The Lotus-Eaters figure
fig_lotus.prompt:
A wide illustration for the pre-fight screen of a mythology card game, showing an enemy in its own scene, made by hand like a 1993 fantasy trading-card or game-book illustration: bold, wobbly black pen-and-ink outlines around every shape, filled with thin, flat, transparent watercolour and gouache washes. Big simple flat shapes of colour with almost no shading or modelling, a little ink cross-hatching in the shadows, blotchy uneven washes with hard dried edges, splatters and visible brush marks, and the rough off-white paper texture and grain clearly showing through the paint. Naive, slightly clumsy, decorative and stylised, like an old printed card with slightly faded, misregistered colour. A limited palette of 4 or 5 colours, dark overall. Absolutely not realistic: no realistic lighting, no glow, no soft gradients, no depth of field, no fine detail or texture rendering, no oil-painting look, no 3D, no digital painting, not modern concept art. Composition: the enemy described below stands in the middle of the scene, full length and large, painted into it with exactly the same outlines, washes, paper grain and palette as everything around it and lit by the scene's own light, so figure and setting are one picture; the setting continues all around it. The bottom strip of the picture stays a little darker and calmer for a name to be written over it. No text, no letters, no border, no frame, no logo, no signature.

Setting: the island of the Lotus-Eaters from Homer's Odyssey at dusk: a drowsy shore of low dunes and tall lotus plants with heavy pale blossoms and honey-coloured fruit, along the left and right edges; a few sleeping sailors slumped among the plants at the far left; a beached Greek ship with its oars abandoned at the far right; thin hazy smoke of poppy incense drifting low; a still, glassy sea and a faint low moon on the horizon.
Colour: deep greens from near-black to moss (#0b1a14 to #2f5a3a) with pale cream blossoms and a few honey-gold accents.

In the scene: A languid Lotus-Eater, a pale, beautiful young man with heavy-lidded dreamy eyes and a crown of lotus blossoms, lounging against a lotus stem and holding out a lotus flower in offering, two others asleep in the reeds behind him. Greek in every detail, as in Homer. A calm, confident, casual pose, at ease: the body turned three-quarters, the head turned to look straight at the viewer. Not attacking, not shouting.

Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Norse look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but colder and harder than the Greek cards. Heavier, rougher black ink lines with a carved, woodcut-like quality, as if cut into wood or stone; flat areas of colour broken by scratchy hatching. A northern base of slate, iron grey, bone white and pine, but every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that dominates the picture: bold and saturated, such as deep blood red, aurora green and violet, velvet purple, ember orange, glacier blue or midnight-sun gold, so the cards never all read as grey-blue. No warm Mediterranean light, no sunsets over a warm sea, no bronze glow. Weather matters: snow, sleet, sea-spray, mist and long winter dusk. Where the picture shows objects, give them Viking Age ornament: interlaced beasts and knotwork carved on wood, iron and runestones in the Urnes and Mammen styles, and the look of the Gotland picture-stones. People are weathered and heavy, in wool, fur, leather and iron; no horned helmets, no winged helmets, no fantasy plate armour. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Viking Age Norse myth: iron mail, round wooden shields, furs, runestones, longhalls, ravens, wolves, fjords, snow and northern sky.

Subject: A standard-bearer: a young warrior holding high a tall pole with a raven banner streaming in the wind, shouting the warband forward.

Composition: a figure caught mid-motion, filling the frame, over the shoulder from behind. Light and colour: storm-dark slate blue with lightning. Presence: an ordinary, humble presence at a modest scale. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Chinese look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but painted in the manner of classical Chinese painting and the illustrated Ming editions of Journey to the West. Fluid, calligraphic brush lines that swell and taper, never hard woodcut or pen hatching. Figures in the fine-line gongbi manner with flat, bold mineral colours (cinnabar red, azurite blue, malachite green, gold); backgrounds in loose xieyi ink wash: misty peaks, pines, waterfalls, splashed ink. Clouds are drawn as curling auspicious-cloud scrolls. Faces and poses are bold and theatrical, like Peking opera. Every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that fills the whole picture, background included: a warm rice-paper ground is only one of many grounds, and most cards should instead be washed in their own colour, such as deep azurite night, jade bamboo green, cinnabar palace red, violet dusk or storm-grey ink, so that no two cards share the same cream background. Brighter and more colourful than the Greek and Norse cards, but never washed out. Not Japanese, not samurai, not anime, not modern Chinese fantasy game art, no restaurant-style dragons. Only paint Sun Wukong himself (golden fur, phoenix-feather cap with long plumes, golden armour, red cape) when the subject names him; any other monkey is an ordinary monkey of Flower-Fruit Mountain with brown or grey fur and simple clothes, never his cap, armour or face. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Journey to the West, classical Chinese myth: silk robes, lacquered armour, temples, clouds, mountains, celestial palaces.

Subject: Myriad staffs: a sky full of hundreds of golden-banded iron staffs raining down like spears onto a heavenly army camp.

Composition: a hand or weapon in the foreground with the effect bursting beyond, from directly above. Light and colour: vermilion and black ink. Presence: an imposing, dramatic presence with strong rim light. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.

composition.shot: a hand or weapon in the foreground with the effect bursting beyond
composition.power: an imposing, dramatic presence with strong rim light

tdum.name: Training Dummy
tdum.prompt:
Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Chinese look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but painted in the manner of classical Chinese painting and the illustrated Ming editions of Journey to the West. Fluid, calligraphic brush lines that swell and taper, never hard woodcut or pen hatching. Figures in the fine-line gongbi manner with flat, bold mineral colours (cinnabar red, azurite blue, malachite green, gold); backgrounds in loose xieyi ink wash: misty peaks, pines, waterfalls, splashed ink. Clouds are drawn as curling auspicious-cloud scrolls. Faces and poses are bold and theatrical, like Peking opera. Every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that fills the whole picture, background included: a warm rice-paper ground is only one of many grounds, and most cards should instead be washed in their own colour, such as deep azurite night, jade bamboo green, cinnabar palace red, violet dusk or storm-grey ink, so that no two cards share the same cream background. Brighter and more colourful than the Greek and Norse cards, but never washed out. Not Japanese, not samurai, not anime, not modern Chinese fantasy game art, no restaurant-style dragons. Only paint Sun Wukong himself (golden fur, phoenix-feather cap with long plumes, golden armour, red cape) when the subject names him; any other monkey is an ordinary monkey of Flower-Fruit Mountain with brown or grey fur and simple clothes, never his cap, armour or face. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature.

Setting: Journey to the West, classical Chinese myth: silk robes, lacquered armour, temples, clouds, mountains, celestial palaces.

Subject: A training dummy in a temple courtyard on Flower-Fruit Mountain: a straw figure on a wooden post wearing a little red headband, its arms made of bamboo poles, scuffed from staff practice, plum blossom falling.

tscr.name: Temple Scribe
tscr.prompt:
Fantasy trading-card illustration in the style of early-to-mid 1990s card art: hand-made traditional media (gouache, acrylic, watercolour and pen-and-ink), visible brushstrokes and pen lines, matte paper texture, and the slightly soft, faded look of a card printed in the 1990s. Expressive and a little stylised rather than realistic: strong shapes, bold silhouettes, sometimes inked outlines and flat patterned colour. Dark overall with near-black shadows, lit by bold, saturated accent colours taken from the card's own light and colour key (no default orange) where they matter. Frame the subject tightly: it fills most of the picture and may be cropped by the edges, with its face or focal point near the centre; keep the background minimal, simple and dark. Landscape 3:2 composition. No text, no letters, no border, no card frame, no logo, no watermark, no signature. Not photorealistic, not 3D render, not modern digital concept art, not anime.

Egyptian look for this hero: the same 1990s hand-made card art, but painted in the manner of ancient Egyptian tomb paintings, temple reliefs and illustrated papyri. Crisp, even, dark outlines around every shape and flat areas of bold mineral colour with very little shading: Egyptian blue, lapis, malachite green, red and yellow ochre, gold leaf, black and white; the faint texture of painted plaster, carved limestone or papyrus fibres shows through. Gods and people may keep the strong Egyptian profile silhouette, but the camera angle still varies from card to card. Ornament comes from Egypt: lotus and papyrus borders, winged sun discs, broad collars, gold and faience. Warm desert and Nile light, between Odin's darkness and Wukong's brightness. Every card has its own strong colour key (given under Light and colour) that fills the picture; Egyptian art is not only blue and gold, so many cards are dominated by red ochre, desert yellow, malachite green, black and white, carnelian or rose. No readable writing: hieroglyphs only as small decorative carving in the background, never as the subject. Not modern Egyptian-themed fantasy game art, not a movie poster, no glowing sci-fi pyramids. Focus over scenery: the card's subject is the star of the picture and should look as striking and powerful as possible, large and unmistakable at a glance. The background is simple, atmospheric and secondary, and no second large figure or creature competes with the subject unless the card is about that creature. Only paint Thoth himself (ibis-headed god with a reed pen and palette) when the subject names him.

Setting: Ancient Egyptian myth of the New Kingdom: temples, tombs, papyrus, the Nile, desert, gods with animal heads, gold, lapis lazuli and faience.

Subject: A temple scribe: a young scribe sitting cross-legged in the classic pose with a papyrus roll across his kilt, a reed pen behind his ear, ink palette at his side, in a sunlit courtyard.

Composition: a figure caught mid-motion, filling the frame, in side profile. Light and colour: temple lamplight amber in darkness. Presence: an ordinary, humble presence at a modest scale. The subject fills most of the picture; keep the background minimal.
